notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 26:1–22, drawn from the sources I was able to access within my search and fetch limits:

---

## v. 1 — "After the plague had ended, the LORD said to Moses and Eleazar…"

The plague of Numbers 25 (the Baal-Peor incident) was the last major calamity to strike Israel before entering Canaan. The phrase "after the plague" marks a turning point — the transition from the doomed first generation to the second generation that would enter the land (Enduring Word, citing Allen). God now speaks to Moses and Eleazar (rather than Moses and Aaron as in the first census, Numbers 1), since Aaron had died and Eleazar had succeeded him as high priest (Gill). The Pulpit Commentary adds that it is improbable the plague specifically wiped out the last survivors of the condemned generation; the plague victims were more likely younger men who joined themselves to Baal-Peor, and "it is part of the moral of the story that these offenders deprived themselves, not merely of a few remaining days, but of many years of happy rest."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-26/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-26.html (Gill)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html (Pulpit)

---

## v. 2 — "Take a census of the whole congregation… all those twenty years of age or older who can serve in the army."

The command mirrors the first census in Numbers 1. Gill notes three purposes: (a) to demonstrate that the old generation had indeed died out as God threatened; (b) to prepare for dividing Canaan proportionally among the tribes; and (c) to show God's faithfulness in multiplying the people despite their sins. The Pulpit Commentary argues the census was not primarily for the war against Midian (which used only 12,000 men, Numbers 31:5) but for the approaching territorial settlement — evident from vv. 52–56. Keil & Delitzsch concur: the census prepared Israel both as "the army of Jehovah" for conquest and for the fair division of land by families, which is why family/clan names are listed (unlike in Numbers 1).

Spurgeon (cited by Enduring Word) saw a pastoral principle: God valued each person individually, "registered by their families and by their names… in the family book of the living God."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-26/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/numbers/26.htm

---

## v. 3 — "So on the plains of Moab by the Jordan, across from Jericho, Moses and Eleazar… issued the instruction."

The location is significant: the plains of Moab, opposite Jericho — Israel is at the threshold of Canaan. The wilderness wanderings are over. Ellicott notes that although the tribal princes who assisted in the first census (Numbers 1:4) are not mentioned here, it is probable a similar arrangement was made. The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary highlights the contrast: the first census was "in the wilderness of Sinai" with the Promised Land far away; this one is "in the plains of Moab, by Jordan, near Jericho" — the land of destiny is now clearly in view.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-26.html (Ellicott)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-26.html (Preacher's Homiletical)

---

## v. 4 — "Take a census of the men twenty years of age or older, as the LORD has commanded Moses. And these were the Israelites who came out of the land of Egypt."

The Cambridge Bible notes that the opening words "Take the sum of the people" are added conjecturally in the English versions, the original Hebrew having lost them. The final clause — "the Israelites who came out of the land of Egypt" — is treated by the Septuagint as a heading for the whole catalogue that follows rather than attached to the preceding sentence (Pulpit Commentary). Gill observes that Moses, when he brought the people out of Egypt, had them committed to him by number; now, about to die, he "delivers them up as it were by number again" (citing Jarchi/Rashi). This contrasts with David's census (2 Samuel 24), which was sinful because David had no divine command for it.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-26.html

---

## vv. 5–7 — Reuben: clans of Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, Carmi; numbered 43,730.

The four clan names agree exactly with Genesis 46:9, Exodus 6:14, and 1 Chronicles 5:3 (Pulpit). The distinguishing feature of this second census is enrollment by families, since the land would be assigned to preserve both tribal and family unity (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary). Reuben's count of 43,730 represents a decline of 2,770 (about 6%) from the first census's 46,500 (Numbers 1:21). Gill notes that this decrease "may in part be accounted for by the families of Dathan and Abiram being cut off for their rebellion."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html

---

## vv. 8–9 — Eliab, son of Pallu; his sons Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram, who fought against Moses and Aaron with Korah's followers.

The genealogy zooms in on Pallu's line because of the notoriety of Dathan and Abiram. The Pulpit Commentary explains that the plural "sons" (בְּנֵי) in v. 8 is a conventional heading for a family list, written before the scribe noted that only one son (Eliab) follows. Enduring Word suggests Dathan and Abiram may have resented Moses's leadership because they were from the tribe of Reuben, Israel's firstborn, whereas Moses was from Levi (a younger son). Allen observes the Hebrew verb for "contended" is rare, "signifying a strong contest of wills," but ultimately they were struggling "not just with man, but with God." 

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-26/

---

## v. 10 — "The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them along with Korah… the fire consumed 250 men. They serve as a warning sign."

The Pulpit Commentary insists the Hebrew here (יַתִּבְלַע אֹתָם וְאֶת־קֹרַח) "seems decisive as to the fate of Korah" — that Korah was swallowed up along with Dathan and Abiram, not consumed by fire. This has been debated because Numbers 16 seems to place Korah with the 250 men offering incense. However, the Pulpit argues it is never clearly stated that Korah died by fire, and that the "obvious meaning" of this verse should stand: Korah was swallowed up. The Hebrew word נֵס (nes, "sign") typically means a banner or ensign; here it means a conspicuous warning for all generations (Cole, cited by Enduring Word). Clarke's Commentary notes that the Samaritan text says Korah was burned, not swallowed, and the fire consumed him with the 250.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-26/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/numbers-26.html (Clarke)

---

## v. 11 — "However, the line of Korah did not die out."

This is one of the more significant verses in the chapter. The Cambridge Bible explains that after Numbers 16 one might naturally infer Korah's whole family perished, but this verse corrects that inference because "in his [the writer's] day 'sons of Korah' were found in Jerusalem" — a Levitical guild that formed part of the temple choirs and produced Psalms 42, 44–49, 84–85, 87–88. Benson (Methodist) says God spared them "because they disowned their father's act, and separated themselves from his tent and company." Matthew Henry draws the application: "If we partake not of the sins of sinners, we shall not partake of their plagues." Jamieson-Fausset-Brown adds that Samuel the prophet was possibly of Korah's line (1 Chronicles 6:22, 33). The Pulpit Commentary notes, however, it is "slightly doubtful" whether the Kohathite Korah who was Samuel's ancestor is identical with the Izharite Korah who was Heman's ancestor.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/26-11.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html

---

## vv. 12–14 — Simeon: clans of Nemuel, Jamin, Jachin, Zerah, Shaul; numbered 22,200.

Simeon's census is the most dramatic in the chapter. From 59,300 at the first census to 22,200 — a devastating loss of 37,100 men (63%). The clan of Ohad (listed in Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15) is missing here; Benson suggests that entire family branch went extinct in the wilderness. Multiple commentators connect Simeon's decline to the Baal-Peor sin: Zimri, who openly brought a Midianite woman into the camp (Numbers 25), was a Simeonite prince. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Simeon is omitted from Moses's blessing in Deuteronomy 33, and its later territory in Canaan was "inconsiderable, only a canton out of Judah's lot" (Joshua 19:9). Some Jewish traditions (cited by Gill from Tanchuma) claim all 24,000 who died in the plague were Simeonites, though Gill deems this unlikely. The Expositor's Bible Commentary adds that Simeon's final allocation of territory was in the district where Kadesh was situated, and "we remember that Simeon and Levi were brethren (Genesis 49:5)."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-26.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/numbers/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-26.html

## vv. 15–18 — Gad: clans of Zephon, Haggi, Shuni, Ozni, Eri, Arod, Areli; numbered 40,500.

Gad counted 40,500, a decline of 5,150 (about 11%) from the first census (45,650). Seven clans are listed, corresponding to Genesis 46:16, though some names have variant spellings (e.g., Ziphion becomes Zephon, Ezbon becomes Ozni). Gill speculates that Gad, being a warlike tribe, "suffered very much in their attempt to enter the land of Canaan contrary to the will of God, and were repulsed and defeated by the Amalekites" (Numbers 14:40–45).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-26.html

---

## v. 19 — "The sons of Judah were Er and Onan, but they died in the land of Canaan."

Er and Onan are mentioned first only to explain their absence. They died childless in Canaan because of their wickedness (Genesis 38:7–10), before the migration to Egypt. The Targum of Jonathan (cited by Gill) adds "because of their sins." Since they founded no families, they do not appear among the clans. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary dryly notes they "were slain by the Lord."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-26.html

---

## vv. 20–21 — Judah's clans: Shelah, Perez, Zerah; and from Perez: Hezron and Hamul.

Three primary families are named: Shelanites (from Shelah), Pharzites (from Perez/Pharez), and Zarhites (from Zerah). The Perez line is further subdivided into Hezronites and Hamulites (Perez's sons). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Pharzites remained a distinct family apart from the Hezronites and Hamulites, suggesting Perez may have had other sons not recorded. Perez and Zerah were the twin sons born to Judah by Tamar (Genesis 38:27–30). The Cambridge Bible notes that the names in this section are based on Genesis 46:8–27, with Ephraim and Manasseh added since they were born in Egypt and could not appear in the Genesis list of those who "went down into Egypt."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/26.htm

---

## v. 22 — "These were the clans of Judah, and their registration numbered 76,500."

Judah's count of 76,500 represents an increase of 1,900 (about 2.5–3%) from the first census's 74,600. Judah is the first tribe listed that grew rather than shrank. Benson comments that this "answers to Jacob's blessing, that he should be a praise among his brethren" (Genesis 49:8). The Pulpit Commentary notes a telling pattern: "all the tribes under the leadership of Judah increased, whilst all those in the camp of Reuben decreased" — Judah's camp (Judah, Issachar, Zebulun) all grew, while Reuben's camp (Reuben, Simeon, Gad) all shrank. The total Israelite fighting force across all tribes went from 603,550 to 601,730 — a net decline of only 1,820 (0.3%), which Enduring Word calls both a sign of "stagnation" (no real growth during 38 years of judgment) and of "God's great mercy" (the wilderness did not destroy them).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/numbers/26.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-26/

## Denominational Distinctives

**On the "sign" (v. 10) and the fate of Korah:** Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan) follows the Samaritan text, maintaining Korah was burned by fire, not swallowed. The Pulpit Commentary (broadly Anglican/evangelical) insists the Hebrew text says Korah was swallowed, and that this meaning should not be forced. This reflects a textual-critical difference, not a doctrinal one, but it surfaces in older commentaries.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html

**On the sons of Korah (v. 11):** Nearly all traditions agree the sons were spared. Benson (Methodist) and Poole (Puritan) emphasize they "disowned their father's act." Matthew Henry (Puritan/Evangelical) draws the moral: separation from sin means separation from judgment. The Cambridge Bible (critical/Anglican) offers the historical explanation — the note was added because the "sons of Korah" were a known temple choir in the writer's day. No major Protestant tradition differs on the doctrinal point; all affirm God does not punish children for their parents' sins if they do not participate (cf. Ezekiel 18).

**On the census purpose:** The Reformed/Calvinistic tradition (Gill, Keil & Delitzsch) strongly emphasizes divine sovereignty — God commanded the census, and the numbers reveal His faithfulness to both judgment and promise. The Baptist tradition (Spurgeon, cited by Enduring Word; Garner-Howes) tends toward the pastoral application: God values each individual. The Pentecostal/Charismatic reading (Enduring Word/David Guzik) emphasizes the spiritual lessons about faith vs. unbelief and the generation that inherited the promise. The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican/homiletical) develops a lengthy parallel between the two censuses and the "twofold election" — election to grace (first census) and election to glory (second census), urging hearers to persevere so their names remain in both.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-26/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-26.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-26.html

---

## Other Views (Limited)

I was unable to fetch Catholic (newadvent.org), Orthodox (oca.org), or modern critical scholarly sources (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) within my search and fetch limits. However, the Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges — which represents a moderate critical Anglican perspective — notes that "the impossibility of the figures is shewn in note on Numbers 1:46," reflecting the mainstream critical view that the census numbers (over 600,000 fighting men, implying a total population of ~2 million) are historically problematic and likely symbolic or idealized.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/26.htm
